ablations.prompt: Tell me why store prices keep climbing, explained for a 10-year-old. Use exactly three bullet points, and grade 5 or lower reading level.

runs.answer:
- **Things cost more to make and move.** Farmers, factories, and truck drivers pay more for fuel, fertilizer, metal, and wages. When it costs more to make a cereal box or bring it to the store, the store often has to charge more for it.

- **People want to buy a lot of stuff.** When lots of people have money and want the same things, stores can raise prices and still sell out. Sometimes there are not enough toys, cars, or houses to go around, so the price goes up.

- **Money gets worth a little less over time.** Banks and governments often make more money available, and each dollar can buy a little less than it used to. So a candy bar that cost one dollar may now cost two, even if the candy stayed the same.

- **Things cost more to make and move.** Farmers, factories, and truck drivers pay more for fuel, workers, and supplies. When it costs more to make a sandwich or a toy, the store has to charge more to cover that.

- **People want to buy a lot, and there aren't always enough things.** When lots of people have money to spend, they buy more stuff. If stores or farms can't make enough right away, the things people want can get pricey, like a popular toy that sells out.

- **Money itself gets a little weaker over time.** Governments and banks often want prices to go up slowly, a little each year. So a dollar buys a bit less than it did before, and stores raise their prices to keep up.

runs.answer:
- Stores pay more to get things made and shipped, like flour, gas for trucks, and workers' paychecks, so they raise prices to cover those costs.
- Sometimes lots of people want the same things at once, and when demand is higher than supply, sellers can charge more.
- Money also loses some value over time, so it takes more dollars to buy the same toy or sandwich as before.

- Things cost more to make and move, like gas for trucks, electricity for factories, and wages for workers, so stores pay more to get their items.
- Sometimes there are shortages, like when not enough of something is grown or built, so people compete for it and prices rise.
- Stores and companies raise prices to cover their higher costs and make a profit, and when lots of people have money to spend, they're willing to pay more.
